title: "Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution"
subtitle: "Where the receivers stand, why spreading them across the field makes the defense show its hand, and why the best modern offenses squeezed them back in."
description: "How to name the spread formations you see every Sunday (2x2, 3x1, empty, bunch, stack, nub and quads), how to number the receivers the way coaches do, why spreading the field forces the defense to declare itself and opens space, why modern NFL offenses condense their splits (crack blocks, the two-way go, rubs), and what wildcat, unbalanced lines and the swinging gate are trying to do."
glossary:
  "2x2": {def: "A formation with two receivers on each side of the ball (counting tight ends and backs who line up outside the tackles). Balanced, so it doesn't tell the defense which side the play is going to.", aliases: ["Doubles"]}
  "3x1": {def: "A formation with three receivers on one side of the ball and one on the other. It overloads one side and isolates the single receiver on the other.", aliases: ["Trips"]}
  Empty: {def: "A formation with nobody in the backfield beside or behind the quarterback: all five eligible receivers line up out wide or on the line, most often three on one side and two on the other (3x2).", aliases: ["3x2"]}
  Bunch: "Three receivers clustered in a tight triangle on one side, usually within two or three yards of each other, with one of them on the line and two just off it."
  Stack: "Two receivers lined up one directly behind the other, the front man on the line and the back man a yard or two behind him."
  Nub: "A side of the formation where a tight end is the only receiver, with no wide receiver outside him. 'Trips nub' puts three receivers on one side and only the tight end on the other."
  Quads: "Four receivers on the same side of the ball. Because only five players can be eligible, quads leaves at most one receiver on the other side."
  "Condensed formation": "A formation in which the receivers line up close to the offensive line (reduced or tight splits) instead of out near the sidelines, to set up crack blocks, two-way gos and rubs, and to make runs and passes look the same."
  "Two-way go": "A receiver with enough room on both sides of the defender covering him that he can break either inside or outside, so the defender has to guess."
  Wildcat: "A formation in which the ball is snapped directly to a running back (or another non-quarterback) standing in the shotgun, while the quarterback lines up as a receiver or leaves the field. Popularized in the NFL by the 2008 Miami Dolphins."
  "Unbalanced line": {def: "An offensive line with more linemen on one side of the center than the other, usually by moving a tackle to line up beside the other tackle ('tackle over'), so one side has an extra blocker.", aliases: ["Tackle over"]}
  "Swinging gate": "A trick alignment, used mostly on extra points and two-point tries, in which the snapper stays over the ball and most of the other linemen line up in a group far out to one side. If the defense doesn't follow, the offense snaps it and attacks the uncovered group; if it does, the offense shifts back into its normal formation."
  "Spread formation": "Any formation that lines its pass-catchers up across the width of the field, toward both sidelines, usually with the quarterback in the shotgun, so the defense has to spread out to cover them. Not the same thing as a 'spread offense,' which is a whole philosophy built on such formations."
  "Receiver numbering": "Counting a formation's receivers from the sideline in, separately on each side: the widest is #1, the next #2, then #3. Defenses assign coverage by these numbers rather than by names."

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (shared helpers for this chapter's diagrams)"}
import os
import shutil

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import animation
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Polygon
from IPython.display import HTML, display

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, routes as r, style, draw_marker
from gridiron.formations import LINE_D, OFF_BALL, TE_W, WING_W, OL_SPLIT

style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")

UC, GUN, TB_D = -1.9, -5.0, -7.0          # QB under center, QB in the shotgun, deep tailback (yards)
TE_RING = style.LINE_TO_GAIN               # gold ring: a tight end (as in the personnel chapter)
RB_RING = style.THIRD                      # aqua ring: a running back
SIDELINE = 26.67                           # yards from the middle of the field to either sideline


def line5():
    """The five offensive linemen, unlettered. (In this chapter "C" always means a cornerback, so the
    center, always the middle lineman, carries no letter.)"""
    return [Player(k, k, "off", LINE_D, w, label="")
            for k, w in [("LT", -2 * OL_SPLIT), ("LG", -OL_SPLIT), ("C", 0.0),
                         ("RG", OL_SPLIT), ("RT", 2 * OL_SPLIT)]]


def P(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    """An offensive player at (d, w): d = yards from the ball (negative = backfield), w = yards to the
    offense's right."""
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label or key)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def check_legal(players):
    """Seven men on the line, and only the two at its ends may be eligible receivers."""
    off = [p for p in players if p.side == "off"]
    line = sorted([p for p in off if abs(p.d - LINE_D) < 0.05], key=lambda p: p.w)
    assert len(off) == 11, f"{len(off)} offensive players"
    assert len(line) == 7, f"{len(line)} on the line: {[p.key for p in line]}"
    for p in line[1:-1]:
        assert p.pos not in ("WR", "TE", "RB", "FB"), f"covered receiver {p.key}"
    return players


def ring_bodies(p):
    """Ring the backs (aqua) and tight ends (gold), so the personnel stays countable."""
    for k, pl in p.players.items():
        if pl.side == "off" and pl.pos in ("RB", "FB"):
            p.highlight(k, color=RB_RING)
        elif pl.side == "off" and pl.pos == "TE":
            p.highlight(k, color=TE_RING)
    return p


def hide_yard_numbers(ax):
    """Drop the faint painted field numbers (they sit where the receivers stand in these zoomed views)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() is not None and abs(t.get_alpha() - 0.55) < 1e-6:
            t.remove()


def pxy(play, fld, d, w):
    x, y = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d, w))
    return float(x), float(y)


def put(ax, play, fld, text, d, w, size=7.5, color=style.INK, ha="center", va="center", weight="normal",
        boxed=True, italic=False):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = pxy(play, fld, d, w)
    kw = dict(bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.5)) if boxed else {}
    ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=size, color=color, ha=ha, va=va, fontweight=weight, zorder=12,
            style="italic" if italic else "normal", linespacing=1.1, **kw)


def shade(ax, play, fld, pts, color, alpha=0.12, ls="-", lw=0.8, z=1.5):
    """Shade a polygon given as (d, w) points."""
    xy = [pxy(play, fld, d, w) for d, w in pts]
    ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=color, ec="none", alpha=alpha, zorder=z))
    ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc="none", ec=color, alpha=min(1.0, alpha * 5), lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=z))


BOX_W, BOX_D = 6.0, 7.5        # the drawn "box": about six yards either side of the ball, 7.5 deep


def shade_box(ax, play, fld):
    shade(ax, play, fld, [(0.3, -BOX_W), (BOX_D, -BOX_W), (BOX_D, BOX_W), (0.3, BOX_W)], style.DEFENSE,
          alpha=0.07, ls=(0, (3, 2)))


def box_count(play):
    return sum(1 for p in play.players.values()
               if p.side == "def" and abs(p.w) <= BOX_W and 0 < p.d <= BOX_D)


def branch(ax, play, fld, pts, color=style.OFFENSE, ls="-", lw=1.7, z=4):
    """A route-style arrow drawn by hand through absolute (d, w) points (used for 'either/or' branches)."""
    xs, ys = zip(*[pxy(play, fld, d, w) for d, w in pts])
    ax.plot(xs[:-1] + (xs[-1],), ys[:-1] + (ys[-1],), color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=z,
            solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2] + 0.8 * (xs[-1] - xs[-2]), ys[-2] + 0.8 * (ys[-1] - ys[-2])),
                                 (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=color, lw=lw,
                                 shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0, zorder=z))


def receiver_numbers(ax, play, fld, d_lab=1.45, size=7.0, at=None):
    """Write #1, #2, #3 ... above each receiver, counting from the sideline in on each side.
    Backs in the backfield (within 3 yards of the ball, behind the line) are not counted. When two
    receivers share a width (a stack), the one on the line counts first. `at` = {key: (d, w)} moves
    a label (for clusters, where the default spots would collide)."""
    at = at or {}
    rec = [p for p in play.players.values() if p.side == "off" and p.pos in ("WR", "TE", "RB", "FB")
           and not (abs(p.w) < 3.0 and p.d < -2.0)]
    for sgn in (-1, 1):
        side = sorted([p for p in rec if p.w * sgn > 0], key=lambda p: (-round(abs(p.w), 1), -p.d))
        for i, p in enumerate(side, 1):
            d, w = at.get(p.key, (d_lab, p.w))
            put(ax, play, fld, f"#{i}", d, w, size=size, color=style.INK_2, boxed=False, weight="bold")


def grid(nrows, ncols, lateral, window, width=6.6, extra=0.38):
    pw = width / ncols
    ph = pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / (lateral[1] - lateral[0]) + extra
    return plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width, nrows * ph), squeeze=False)


def title(ax, text, sub=None):
    ax.set_title(text, loc="left", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, pad=3)
    if sub:
        ax.text(1.0, 1.0, sub, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=7.5,
                color=style.INK_2)


# --- One personnel grouping (11: one back, one tight end, three receivers), eight formations. ------------
# Every alignment below is legal: check_legal() confirms seven on the line with receivers only at the ends.
def form(name):
    q, rb = P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R")
    f = {
        "2x2": [q, rb, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.5), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -8.5),
                P("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 8.5), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 15.5)],
        "3x1": [q, rb, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.5), P("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 7.0),
                P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 11.2), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 15.5)],
        "trey": [q, rb, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.5), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
                 P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 10.0), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 15.5)],
        "empty": [q, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.5), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -8.5),
                  P("RB", "RB", OFF_BALL, 6.0, "R"), P("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 10.5), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 15.5)],
        "bunch": [q, rb, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.5), P("H", "WR", LINE_D, 8.6),
                  P("Y", "TE", -2.2, 7.2), P("Z", "WR", -2.2, 10.0)],
        "stack": [q, rb, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.5), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -8.5),
                  P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 11.0), P("Y", "TE", -2.5, 11.0)],
        "nub": [q, P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, -TE_W), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 7.0),
                P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 11.2), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, 15.5)],
        "quads": [q, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.5), P("RB", "RB", OFF_BALL, 5.8, "R"),
                  P("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 9.1), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 12.4), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 15.8)],
    }[name]
    return check_legal(line5() + [p.moved() for p in f])


PLATE_LAT, PLATE_WIN = (-17.6, 17.6), (-7.0, 3.0)


def plate(ax, name, head, sub, numbers=True, lateral=PLATE_LAT, window=PLATE_WIN, at=None):
    p = ring_bodies(Play(form(name), None, los=40, to_go=None))
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    if numbers:
        receiver_numbers(ax, p, fld, at=at)
    title(ax, head, sub)
    return p, fld


def ring_legend(fig, y=0.0):
    h = [Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=8, markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE, markeredgecolor=RB_RING,
                markeredgewidth=2.0, label="running back (R)"),
         Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=8, markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE, markeredgecolor=TE_RING,
                markeredgewidth=2.0, label="tight end (Y)"),
         Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=8, markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE, markeredgecolor="white",
                label="wide receivers X, Z, H; Q = quarterback")]
    fig.legend(handles=h, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, y), ncol=3, fontsize=7.5, frameon=False,
               handletextpad=0.3, columnspacing=1.2)


# --- Frame strips (PDF) and videos (web) for the two animations. ------------------------------------------
MARK_R = 0.62


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=()):
    """One moment of a simulated play: markers, trails, rings."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=True,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.5, play.los + window[1] - 0.5)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.5, yhi - 0.5)]
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(set(shown["_id"])) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for key, col in rings:
        rr = cur[cur["displayName"] == key]
        if len(rr):
            x, y = fld.xy(rr["x"].iloc[0], rr["y"].iloc[0])
            ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), MARK_R * 1.65, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
    for _, row in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(row["x"], row["y"]))
        if row["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.5), 0.75, 0.45, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=11))
            continue
        draw_marker(ax, x, y, row["side"], row["label"], ppy, r=MARK_R)
    return fld


def strip(play, times, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), ncols=2, width_in=6.5):
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False, figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + 0.55)))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"), fontsize=8.5,
                     color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        ax.text(0.5, -0.02, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.4,
                color=style.INK, linespacing=1.15)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2.2, w_pad=0.8)
    return fig


def video(play, times, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), width_in=5.6):
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.45))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        cur = [n for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
        txt = ("snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s") + (("   " + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else "")
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=sorted(df["frameId"].unique()), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def animated(play, times, notes, lateral, window, rings=()):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if PDF:
        strip(play, times, notes, lateral, window, rings)
        plt.show()
    else:
        video(play, times, notes, lateral, window, rings)
```

Third-and-6, midway through the second quarter. The offense breaks the huddle and the running back
doesn't stop behind the quarterback. He keeps jogging, out past the right tackle, and settles in the
slot just inside the tight end, who is himself standing ten yards from the ball. Nobody is left
beside the quarterback. Five players are spread across the width of the field, and the defense
starts to move: a linebacker drifts out after the running back, a safety creeps down toward the
line, a cornerback points and shouts. The analyst says "empty set, they're going to make the
defense show its hand." Two series later the same offense lines up with all three of its wide
receivers squeezed in tight, the nearest one barely four yards outside the tackle, and the analyst
says "look how condensed they are." Same team, same players, opposite pictures. This chapter
explains both: what the spread formations are, why spreading players across the field makes a
defense commit, and why so many of the best NFL offenses then pulled their receivers back in.

**You'll be able to…**

- Name the spread formations you'll see every week, 2x2, 3x1 (trips), empty, bunch, stack, nub and
  quads, in a glance, and number the receivers on each side the way coaches do.
- Explain why spreading receivers across the field forces the defense to declare itself and opens
  space, and what the offense gives up to get that.
- Count receivers against defenders on each side before the snap, with a three-step rule, and say
  where the offense has the numbers.
- Tell a condensed formation from a spread one (and from the old tight formations), and explain why
  modern offenses squeeze their receivers in: crack blocks, the two-way go, rubs, and plays that all
  look alike.
- Recognize three specialty looks, wildcat, the unbalanced line and the swinging gate, and say what
  each one is trying to make the defense do.
- Read what the data says about how often NFL teams line up with an empty backfield, and when.

Three ideas from [Formation Rules and the Language of
Alignment](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) run through this chapter, so here they are in
one line each. **Seven players must be on the line of scrimmage**, and only the two at the ends of
that line can catch a pass; everyone else is a yard or more behind it, "off the line." **The
letters** name spots, not body types: X is the receiver on the line on one side, Z the receiver off
the line on the other, Y usually the tight end, H a slot receiver or second back. A
[split](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) is how far a receiver lines up from the ball
or the nearest lineman, and a [slot](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) receiver is one
who lines up between the outside receiver and the line. And remember the last chapter's rule:
[personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) is *who* is on the field. Formation, this chapter's
subject, is *where they stand*.

## What makes a formation "spread"

A formation is a picture of where the eleven offensive players stand at the snap. For most of
football history that picture was compact: the receivers lined up a few yards outside the tackles,
the quarterback was under center, and two backs stood behind him. The [classic
formations](02-03-classic-formations.qmd), the I, the pro set and the singleback, are all built
that way, and they are built to run the ball with as many blockers near it as possible.

A [**spread formation**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spread-formation) does the
opposite. It takes the players who can catch passes and spreads them out across the width of the field, toward both sidelines, usually with the quarterback a few
yards back in the [shotgun](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) so he can see it all. Nothing
about the personnel has to change. The same eleven players can line up either way:

``` {.python .cell-code}
tight = check_legal(line5() + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"),
                               P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, WING_W + 0.4),
                               P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 10.5), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -9.0)])
d_tight = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.7, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.4),
           D("SS", "SS", 6.8, 3.9), D("NB", "NB", 4.0, 8.2, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -9.5),
           D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 11.5), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -1.0)]
spread = form("2x2")
d_spread = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
            D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.0),
            D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.2, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 7.5, 7.6), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5),
            D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0)]
LAT, WIN = (-18, 18), (-8.5, 14.6)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN)
for ax, off, dfn, head in [(axes[0, 0], tight, d_tight, "Tight"), (axes[0, 1], spread, d_spread, "Spread (2x2)")]:
    p = ring_bodies(Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None))
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    shade_box(ax, p, fld)
    put(ax, p, fld, f"{box_count(p)} in the box", 9.8, -9.5, size=8,
        weight="bold", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

:::
:::


Look at what the spread did to the defense without anybody running a step. On the left, the
defense can keep seven players in the [box](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd): the area near the
ball, roughly between the ends of the offensive line and within about seven yards of it, where the
defenders who stop runs stand. (The full definition, and the habit of counting the box before every
snap, belong to [A First Look at Defense](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd).) On the right, the offense has put four players out
toward the sidelines. Each of them is a threat to catch a pass, so each needs a defender somewhere
near him, and those defenders have to come from somewhere. They come out of the box. Now there are
six.

That is the first and most basic reason spread formations exist. **The field is 53⅓ yards wide, and
a spread formation makes the defense defend all of it.** Every defender who leaves the middle to
cover a receiver out wide is a defender who isn't there to tackle a runner or to rush the
quarterback.

There are three more reasons, and they are what the rest of this chapter is about.

**Spreading out makes the defense declare itself.** When receivers stand close together, defenders
can stand close together too, in a clump that hides what they plan to do. When the receivers spread
out, the defenders have to spread with them, and where they go is information. A cornerback who
follows a receiver all the way across the field is probably playing man-to-man, each defender
assigned to one receiver, rather than zone, each defender assigned to an area of the field (both
are introduced properly in [A First Look at Defense](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)). A safety who walks
down toward a slot receiver has told you he isn't going to be deep. A linebacker who stays in the
box has told you somebody outside is uncovered or covered by someone farther away. The quarterback
reads all of that before the snap. So can you.

**Spreading out creates space.** A receiver near the sideline with one defender in front of him and
nobody else within fifteen yards is in a one-on-one race. A quick throw to him, or a run through a
box with six defenders instead of eight, gives the ball carrier room to make one man miss.

**Spreading out simplifies the quarterback's job.** With receivers spaced widely, each pass-catcher
occupies his own patch of grass, and the quarterback can see who is open by seeing where the
defenders *aren't*.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**Spread formations exist to make the defense cover the whole field and tell you how it plans to do
it.** They trade blockers near the ball for space away from it. What the offense gives up is the
old advantages of tight formations: extra blockers at the [point of
attack](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) (the spot where the run is aimed), a quarterback under
center who can hand off and fake quickly, and a run game that can simply outnumber the defense. A
spread offense can still run, often very well, but it runs by making the box *lighter*, not by
bringing more bodies to it.
:::

### Formation, not philosophy

A *spread formation* is a picture at the snap: receivers out wide. A [spread
offense](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd) is a whole philosophy, born mostly in
college, built on those pictures. Every NFL team uses spread formations every week; only some would
call their offense a spread offense. This chapter is about the pictures. The philosophy has its own
chapter in [The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd), and the systems
that grew out of it, like the [Air
Raid](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd), are installed in Part 4.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"Spread means pass."** Spreading out makes the defense lighter in the box, which is good for
*running*. Many college spread offenses were built to run first, and in the NFL, 11-personnel
formations with three receivers spread out are only slightly pass-leaning (about 56% pass in neutral
situations, as [Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) showed). The one spread formation that
really does mean "pass," the empty backfield, is the exception, and we'll
measure it below.
:::

## The question every spread formation asks

Spread formations work because they force the defense to answer a question it would rather not
answer. Here is the cleanest version of it. The offense lines up in a 2x2 (two receivers on each
side). On the right, the slot receiver is the tight end, Y. The defense has a cornerback on each
outside receiver, a fifth defensive back (the nickel back, $) on the left slot, and two safeties
deep. Who covers Y?

::: {#cell-fig-slot-dilemma .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def dilemma(w_out):
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, -1.4),
           D("WILL", "WILL", 4.3, 7.0) if w_out else D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, 2.4),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.2, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5),
           D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -9.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 9.0)]
    p = ring_bodies(Play(form("2x2"), dfn, los=40, to_go=None))
    p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
    if w_out:
        p.handoff("RB", t=0.5)
        p.run("RB", [(1.5, 2.0), (6.0, 2.4), (10.5, 1.6)], delay=0.15)
    else:
        p.route("Y", r.hitch(6))
        p.pass_to("Y", t=1.3)
    return p


LAT, WIN = (-18, 18), (-7.5, 14.0)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN)
for ax, w_out, head in [(axes[0, 0], False, "W stays inside"), (axes[0, 1], True, "W walks out")]:
    p = dilemma(w_out)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    shade_box(ax, p, fld)
    n = box_count(p)
    put(ax, p, fld, f"{n} in the box", 9.6, -1.0, size=7.6, weight="bold", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
    put(ax, p, fld, "run it" if w_out else "throw to Y", 9.6, -10.0 if w_out else 12.6, size=7.6,
        weight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The box has six defenders, but Y has nobody within seven yards of him, so the quarterback throws him a quick pass: a hitch, six yards up the field and a turn back to the ball. Right: W walks out over Y to take that throw away. Now the box has five defenders against five offensive linemen, and the offense hands the ball off. Shaded rectangle = the box; the safeties (FS, SS) are deep, 12 yards off the ball.](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations_files/figure-html/fig-slot-dilemma-output-1.svg){#fig-slot-dilemma}

If the linebacker stays inside, the box is solid against the run but the tight end is alone, and a
five-yard throw to him is as easy as a handoff. If he walks out, he takes the throw away and leaves
five defenders in the box to face five blockers. Every lineman now has someone to block, and the
first defender the running back has to beat is a safety twelve yards away. The defense can't
be right both ways, because one player can't stand in two places. The offense watches where he
stands and does the other thing.

That defender, the one stuck between the box and a slot receiver, is so important that he has his
own names. A defender who stands halfway between the end of the line and the slot is "at the
[apex](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)" (the point of the triangle the three of them make), and
the man outside the box but inside a receiver is the [overhang
defender](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd), because he hangs over the edge of the box. The passing
game builds whole plays around reading him. (The name for a defender with two jobs and time for only one is a [conflict
defender](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd); you'll meet him again in
[RPOs](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd), run-pass options in which the quarterback decides after
the snap whether to hand off or throw, and which turn this exact question into a play.) For now,
notice that the *formation* created the question. In the tight formation there was no slot
receiver, so there was no question.

The defense isn't helpless, of course. It can bring a safety down to help, which leaves less help
deep. It can play a coverage in which the outside cornerback and the linebacker trade
responsibilities. It can disguise its answer and change it at the snap. Those are the defense's
moves, and Parts 5 to 7 are full of them. But every one of them costs something somewhere else on
the field, and the spread's whole idea is to make the defense pay that cost on every snap.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In *Madden*, the defense lines itself up: you pick a play, and the computer slides every defender
into place against whatever formation the offense shows. Real defenses have to do that themselves,
in about the ten seconds between the offense breaking the huddle and the snap. They do it with
**rules agreed in advance**: "against 2x2, the nickel takes the slot to the field and the Will
takes the other one; against trips, the safety rotates down." The middle linebacker and the safeties
shout those adjustments to everyone else, and they all have to hear and agree. That's why offenses
love formations the defense hasn't prepared for, and why a defense that sees a formation it didn't
practice sometimes ends up with two players covering one receiver and nobody on another.
:::

## Counting receivers: #1, #2, #3

You met the coaches' counting system in [Formation Rules](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd),
and every formation name in this chapter is built on it, so here it is again with a name.
[**Receiver numbering**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-receiver-numbering) counts the receivers
from the sideline in, separately on each side of the ball. The widest receiver on a side is **#1**,
the next one in is **#2**, the next is **#3**. It doesn't matter whether he's a wide receiver, a
tight end or a running back who has lined up out wide: if he's out of the backfield, he gets a
number. A back standing beside or behind the quarterback isn't counted until he leaves.

Why number them instead of using names? Because the defense doesn't care who the receivers are; it
cares where they are. A coverage rule like "the nickel back takes #2" works against any formation
and any personnel. The numbers also give a formation its name: two on each side is "2x2," three on
one side and one on the other is "3x1." The side with more receivers is the [passing
strength](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) you met in the last chapter.

Two wrinkles, because defenses don't all count the same way. Many coverage systems give an offset
back (one standing to one side of the quarterback) the next number on his side *before* the snap,
#3 beside two receivers, because he can release there in a step. And the count is redone after
every [motion](02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd): a receiver who motions across the formation changes
both sides' numbers, so the player who was "#2 right" in the huddle can be "#3 left" at the snap.
That re-counting, under a play clock, is one reason offenses motion so much.

Here are the four formations you'll see most, all with the same 11 personnel:

::: {#cell-fig-core-plates .cell execution_count=4}

``` {.python .cell-code}
fig.set_size_inches(6.6, fig.get_size_inches()[1] + 0.3)
plate(axes[0, 0], "2x2", "2x2 (doubles)", "2 + 2")
plate(axes[0, 1], "3x1", "3x1 (trips)", "1 + 3")
plate(axes[1, 0], "trey", "3x1 with the TE attached (trey)", "1 + 3")
plate(axes[1, 1], "empty", "Empty (3x2)", "2 + 3, nobody in the backfield")

ring_legend(fig)
```

The names vary by team. One staff's "Doubles" is another's "Deuce" or "Spread"; "Trips" is also

uses the numbers.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"Trips means three wide receivers."** It means three *receivers* on one side, whatever their
position. In the plate above, the third receiver in trips is a tight end, and in empty the third man
on the right is the running back. Personnel counts bodies; formations count *spots*. When the
broadcast says "11 personnel, trips right," that's two separate facts: who is on the field, and
where three of them are standing.
:::

## 2x2: balance

A [**2x2**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-2x2) formation, also called
[**doubles**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-doubles), has two receivers on each side of the ball.
In the most common NFL version the outside receivers (#1s, X and Z) stand on the line near the
sidelines and the inside receivers (#2s, the slots) stand off the line, a few yards inside them.
The slots *must* be off the line: if a slot receiver stood on the line, the outside receiver would
be "covered" (no longer at the end of the line) and couldn't legally catch a pass. That's the
[covered receiver](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) rule, and it's why you'll almost
always see a slot receiver a step behind the receiver outside him.

The 2x2's virtue is **balance**. The defense can't tell from the alignment which side the play is
going to, because the two sides look alike. The offense can run the same route combination to
both sides, called a "mirrored" concept, and let the quarterback pick whichever side the defense
covers worse. Or it can run two *different* combinations and pick based on what the defense shows.
Against a defense with two deep safeties, a 2x2 asks each safety to help on his own side, two
receivers apiece, and a defense that wants to bring an extra defender into the box has to decide
which side gets less help.

What 2x2 gives up is **concentration**. Because the formation is balanced, the defense can be
balanced too: it can play the same coverage to both sides with the same number of defenders, and
nothing about the alignment forces it to shift. The formations that follow all trade some of that
balance for an advantage somewhere specific.

## 3x1: the overload

Put three receivers on one side and one on the other, and you have a
[**3x1**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3x1) formation, almost universally called
[**trips**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-trips). It's the formation of the opening play in
[What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd), "Gun Trips Right," and
it's one of the most common pictures in the NFL.

Trips does two things at once. On the three-receiver side, the *trips side*, it puts more
receivers than the defense normally has defenders, so the defense has to send help. On the other
side, the *backside*, it leaves one receiver, often the offense's best, alone with one cornerback.

To see the problem, you need a way to count a side. Here's the one this book uses, every time:

1. **Count the receivers** on that side (#1, #2, #3).
2. **Count the underneath defenders** who could cover them: everyone on that side who stands
   *outside the box*, including an apex or overhang defender walked out toward a slot. Defenders
   inside the box don't count; they're there for the run.
3. **Note the deep safety** on that side separately, as help over the top ("+ safety"). He's too
   deep to stop a quick throw, but he matters on anything thrown down the field.

If step 1 beats step 2, the offense has a numbers advantage underneath, and a quick throw to that
side is waiting. The defense has to choose which side's problem to solve:

::: {#cell-fig-trips-choice .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def trips_d(rotate):
    common = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
              D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, -0.6),
              D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5), D("NB", "NB", 5.0, 11.6, "$")]
    if rotate:
        return common + [D("WILL", "WILL", 4.4, 6.6), D("SS", "SS", 7.5, 9.2), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -9.0)]
    return common + [D("WILL", "WILL", 4.4, 6.6), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 9.5), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -9.0)]


LAT, WIN = (-18, 18), (-7.4, 16.5)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN)
for ax, rot, head in [(axes[0, 0], False, "Stay balanced"), (axes[0, 1], True, "Rotate to trips")]:
    p = ring_bodies(Play(form("3x1"), trips_d(rot), los=40, to_go=None))
    if rot:
        p.drop("FS", (14.0, 0.5))
        p.highlight("X", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    if rot:
        put(ax, p, fld, "X alone:\none-on-one", -4.8, -11.5, size=7.2, weight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
        put(ax, p, fld, "3 receivers vs\n4 defenders", -4.8, 11.5, size=7.2)
    else:
        put(ax, p, fld, "1 receiver vs\nC + safety", -4.8, -11.5, size=7.2)
        put(ax, p, fld, "3 receivers vs\n3 + safety", -4.8, 11.5, size=7.2)
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Counted the three-step way, the three receivers on the right face three underneath defenders (the cornerback C, the nickel back $ and the linebacker W, walked out to the apex over Y) plus a deep safety, and the lone receiver X on the left has his cornerback and a safety over the top. Right: the defense rotates toward trips. The left safety (FS) moves to the deep middle and the right safety (SS) comes down between H and Y, so the trips side now has four underneath defenders against three receivers, but X is one-on-one with no safety on his side of the field. Either way the defense has given something up.](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations_files/figure-html/fig-trips-choice-output-1.svg){#fig-trips-choice}

:::


If the defense stays balanced, the trips side is three receivers against three defenders underneath
and one safety, and the offense can attack it with combinations designed to put two receivers on
one defender. If the defense rotates, it gets an extra man to the trips side, but the backside
receiver is now alone on what coaches call an *island*, one-on-one with nobody behind his
cornerback. That's why offenses so often put their best receiver at the single-receiver spot in
3x1. They're betting he wins one-on-one, and if the defense refuses that bet by keeping a safety on
his side, the trips side is short-handed.

Many modern defenses have a third answer. They keep both safeties deep before the snap, so the
picture still looks balanced, and then let the *backside* safety leave X to his cornerback and drift
across to help on the trips side's #3 if he runs deep. Coaches call it
[poach](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd), and it and its cousins are the subject of
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd).
It looks like a better deal, but count it: X is still on an island. Every answer to trips spends
the backside safety somewhere.

The trade-off for the offense is that **trips announces its strength**. The defense knows which
side has the numbers and can tilt its coverage, its front and its blitzes (extra pass rushers; see
[A First Look at Defense](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)) toward it. Trips also
leaves the backside thin for the run game: with only one receiver over there, the defense can
squeeze its run defenders toward the trips side without worrying much about a quick throw the
other way. Offenses answer by running *away* from trips, toward the single receiver, where the
defense has thinned out; the run game chapters show how.

Trips also interacts with the hash. With the ball on a hash mark, one side of the field is about
six yards wider than the other (the [field side and the boundary
side](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd)). Most offenses put trips to the field
side, where three receivers have room to spread out, and leave the single receiver to the short
side. When an offense puts trips into the *boundary*, squeezing three receivers into the narrow side,
it's usually a deliberate surprise: the defense's rules for the field and the boundary may not fit.

## Empty: everyone out

An [**empty**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-empty) formation has nobody in the backfield but
the quarterback. All five eligible receivers are out, most often three on one side and two on the
other, so it's also called [**3x2**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3x2) (and "5-wide" on
broadcasts). As the plates above showed, empty usually isn't a special personnel grouping. The
running back and tight end simply line up as receivers. In 2025, about 72% of NFL empty snaps came
from ordinary 11 personnel.[^empty-pers]

Empty is the spread taken to its limit, and it does three things nothing else does.

**It shows the quarterback everything.** With five receivers spread out, the defense has to put
someone near each of them, and the quarterback can often make a good guess at man coverage or zone
before the snap by watching who goes where. Where a defender lines up isn't enough on its own (a
linebacker walked out over the back can be playing a zone area just as easily as the back himself),
but how he lines up and moves is. A defender who presses the receiver or sits on his inside
shoulder with his eyes on *him* is usually in man; one who stands off with his eyes on the
quarterback is usually in zone. And if the back motions and a linebacker has to run across the field
with him, that's a strong man tell, the trick [Motion and Shifts](02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd) builds
on.

**It isolates the backs and tight ends.** A running back split out wide is often covered by a
linebacker, who is bigger and slower than the defensive backs. If the defense brings in more
defensive backs to cover him, it is smaller everywhere else.

**It exposes the blitz.** Five receivers out means only the five offensive linemen are left to
block. If the defense shows six pass rushers, everyone in the stadium can count: five blockers,
six rushers, one man free. The protection decides *which* man: it usually blocks from the inside out
and leaves the widest rusher, because he has the longest way to run. The quarterback knows it in
advance, so the answer is built into the play: get the ball out before the free man arrives, to a
receiver running into the space a blitzer just left. Coaches call that a [hot
route](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd), and a receiver who sees the blitz and cuts
his route short for it is making a [sight
adjust](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd); you'll hear both words on broadcasts.

::: {#cell-fig-empty-pressure .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
emp = form("empty")

         D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.6, -2.4), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.6, 0.8),
         D("LCB", "CB", 3.0, -15.5), D("NB", "NB", 3.5, -9.0, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 4.5, 6.2),
         D("DB", "DB", 4.0, 10.9, "D"), D("RCB", "CB", 3.0, 15.5)]

# Inside-out protection: five blockers each step to one rusher; the widest rusher (the end on the left)
# is the sixth man, and nobody has him. Drawn the playbook way: each rusher's arrow stops at his blocker.
for ol, dk, w_meet in [("LT", "WILL", -3.1), ("LG", "WDT", -1.3), ("C", "MIKE", 0.4),

    d_ = p.players[dk]
    p.rush(dk, pts=[(0.05 - d_.d, w_meet - d_.w)])

p.dropback(1.0)
p.route("H", r.slant(1.0, 6.0))
p.pass_to("H", t=0.85)
p.highlight("WDE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-18, 18), window=(-8.0, 9.0), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
```

The trade-offs are just as clear. Empty leaves nobody to pick up a blitzer, so the quarterback has to
throw quickly and accurately every time the defense brings pressure, and some of those throws are
short of the first-down marker. It makes the run game nearly disappear: there's no back to hand
off to, so the only run left is the quarterback himself. And it is the most **predictable**
formation in the spread family, because everyone knows what it's for.

How predictable? Here is the empty-backfield rate in the NFL over the last decade, measured two
ways, and what offenses did from it. (Empty is the only formation in this chapter the free
play-by-play data can see; there's no free season-by-season count of 2x2 against 3x1.[^no-2x2])

Two numbers tell the story. First, empty is a *specialty* formation: between about 7 and 9.5
percent of plays, every season for a decade, with no steady trend either way. Second, it is
overwhelmingly a passing formation: in 2023–2025, more than 94% of NFL plays from empty were
dropbacks, against about 58% from everything else.[^empty-data] Offenses save it for third down, and
especially third-and-long, when they need a completion and a run would rarely get the yards anyway.

What about the dip to a decade low in 2025? It came in the same season that 11 personnel, the
grouping most empty snaps come from, fell to a decade low of its own ([Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)
tells that story). But the mix explains only a little of it. Offenses also went empty less often
*from* 11 personnel: about 10.6% of 11-personnel snaps were empty in 2024, and 8.6% in
2025.[^empty-2025] One season is a blip until the next one confirms it.

That predictability is the price, and it's why empty is a *tool* rather than a base formation. If
empty is almost always a pass, the defense can rush the passer without worrying about the run.
Offenses that use it a lot find ways to make it less predictable, and the best way is a quarterback
who is dangerous running the ball. The Buffalo Bills under Josh Allen have gone empty on about 10% of
their plays since 2019, against a league rate of about 8%, and in 2023 about one in eight of their
empty snaps was a designed run, nearly all by Allen, more than twice the rate for the rest of the
league.[^bills] Why that works is the second drill at the end of the chapter.

Top right: stack, two receivers one directly behind the other (Z on the line, Y behind him); with no difference in width, the man on the line counts first. Bottom left: trips nub, three receivers to the right and only the tight end on the left, attached to the line with nobody outside him. Bottom right: quads, four receivers on the right (the back, R, among them) and X alone on the left, with nobody beside the quarterback.](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations_files/figure-html/fig-variant-plates-output-1.svg){#fig-variant-plates}
:::
:::


A [**bunch**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bunch) is three receivers clustered in a tight
triangle, usually within two or three yards of each other: one on the line (the "point"), the other
two just off it, one inside and one outside. A [**stack**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stack)
is two receivers lined up one directly behind the other, the front man on the line and the back man
a yard or two behind. Both are legal for the same reason as everything else in this chapter: only
one receiver in each cluster is on the line, and he's the end of it.

Clusters are where numbering gets awkward, so it's worth a rule. Count by width, as always: in the
bunch above, Z is the widest (#1), the point man H is #2 and Y, tucked inside, is #3. In a stack the
two receivers share a width, and most staffs count the man on the line as #1 and the man behind
him as #2. Don't expect the numbers to hold for long, though. Many defenses facing a cluster
number it *after* the snap, by who releases where ("whoever goes out is #1"), which is exactly
the kind of on-the-fly agreement the cluster is designed to strain.

Why would an offense that wants space squeeze its receivers together? Three reasons, and they all
have to do with defenses that play man-to-man.

**Traffic.** In man coverage, each defender follows one receiver wherever he goes. When three
receivers start within two yards of each other and then run in different directions, their paths
cross, and the defenders chasing them have to get around each other and around the other
receivers. A defender who is a step late is a receiver who is a step open. Watch the ringed safety:

::: {#cell-fig-bunch-traffic .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
bunch_off = form("bunch")
bunch_def = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
             D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, -0.5), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, 3.0),
             D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -16), D("RCB", "CB", 5.0, 12.2), D("NB", "NB", 4.2, 9.6, "$"),
             D("SS", "SS", 5.2, 6.2), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, 0.0)]
bp = Play(bunch_off, bunch_def, los=40, to_go=None)
bp.route("H", [(0, 0), (5.5, 0), (10.5, 5.5)])                # point man climbs, then breaks to the corner
bp.route("Z", [(0, 0), (2.2, 0), (5.2, -5.0)])                # outside man cuts in, under the point man
bp.route("Y", [(0, 0), (2.4, 4.4), (3.2, 9.3), (6.2, 10.8)])  # inside man to the flat, crossing under both
# Man defenders, drawn by hand. The nickel and the corner chase their men; the safety on Y can't go
# straight through the bunch, so he bends back over the top of the traffic and arrives late.
bp.path("NB", [(5.6, 10.0), (7.2, 10.6), (9.0, 12.4)], absolute=True, speed=5.8, delay=0.2)    # trails H
bp.path("RCB", [(4.2, 11.0), (3.0, 8.4), (2.6, 6.4)], absolute=True, speed=5.4, delay=0.25)    # chases Z
bp.path("SS", [(5.4, 7.0), (6.8, 8.4), (5.0, 11.4), (3.4, 14.4), (2.2, 16.6)], absolute=True, speed=5.4,
        delay=0.35)
bp.dropback(1.5)
bp.pass_to("Y", t=1.0)
T_CATCH = next(t for t in np.arange(1.0, 3.0, 0.05)
               if np.linalg.norm(bp.ball_position(t) - bp.position("Y", t)) < 0.3)
BUNCH_T = [0.0, 0.6, 1.2, float(np.ceil(T_CATCH * 10) / 10)]
SS_GAP = float(np.linalg.norm(bp.position("SS", BUNCH_T[-1]) - bp.position("Y", BUNCH_T[-1])))
assert SS_GAP > 2.5, SS_GAP                                     # the caption says "about three yards away"
BUNCH_NOTES = ["Snap: each defender has\none receiver in the triangle",
               "H climbs, Z cuts under him,\nY heads out: the paths cross",
               "The safety on Y has to bend\nover the top of the traffic",
               "The ball reaches Y with his\ndefender three yards away"]
animated(bp, BUNCH_T, BUNCH_NOTES, lateral=(-5.0, 23.0), window=(-8.0, 15.0),
         rings=(("Y", TE_RING), ("SS", style.DEFENSE)))
```

Bunch against man coverage (simulated, BDB-format tracking). Ringed: the tight end Y and the safety (SS) assigned to him. 1: each receiver in the bunch has one defender: the cornerback (C) on Z, the nickel ($) on H, the safety on Y. 2: H climbs, Z cuts inside underneath him and Y heads for the flat, so their paths cross right at the line, where the defenders have to get through them. 3: the safety can't go straight to Y; H and the defenders chasing H and Z are in his way, so he has to bend back over the top of them. 4: the ball arrives at Y in the flat with his defender still about three yards away. Nobody blocked anybody; the alignment did the work.
:::
:::


The receivers never touched the defenders, and that matters. Running into a defender on purpose to
knock him off a receiver, after the snap and before the pass is touched, more than a yard past the
line of scrimmage, is offensive pass interference.[^opi] Read that rule closely and you can see how
bunch plays are built. Contact *within* a yard of the line isn't pass interference, which is one
reason the crossings in a bunch release happen right at the line, as they do in the strip above.
Past that yard, the receivers' own paths have to do the work: each one runs his route exactly as
drawn, and if a defender has to go around him, that's the defender's problem. Officials have to
judge the difference between a receiver running his route ("natural pick," or "rub") and a receiver
who goes looking for a defender to block, and the second one draws a flag. The full family of [rub
routes](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) is in [Dropback
Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd).

**Free releases.** A cornerback who wants to jam a receiver at the line (to
[press](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) him) has to
line up right in front of him. In a stack, only the front receiver can be pressed; the man behind
him starts with a free run. In a bunch, the two back receivers are shielded in the same way. That
makes clusters a favorite answer to defenses that press.

**Communication.** Clustered receivers force defenders to decide, at the snap, who takes whom.
Many defenses don't try to follow their man through the traffic; they agree to *switch* (coaches
also say "swap"), so the
defender nearest the receiver going out takes him and the defender nearest the receiver going in
takes that one. Switching works, but it takes two defenders who see the same thing at the same time
and talk. Every time a defense has to communicate under stress, it can get it wrong.

What clusters give up is **width**. Three receivers within three yards of each other can be covered
by fewer zone defenders than three receivers spread across the field, because a zone defender
standing in the right spot can cover two of them. That's why bunch and stack are at their best
against man coverage, and why you'll see them most in the [red
zone](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) and on third-and-short, where
defenses play the most man. They aren't useless against zone, though: three receivers released from
one spot can flood one defender's area at three depths (short, middle and deep), and he can only
cover one of them.

Andy Reid's Kansas City Chiefs are the best-known modern users, stacking and bunching receivers
(often with Travis Kelce in the cluster) as an answer to man coverage; both of their
fourth-quarter touchdowns in Super Bowl LVII came from a stack with a receiver tucked behind
another, though the trick that beat the man coverage was the return motion you'll meet in [Motion and Shifts](02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd).[^chiefs]

## Lopsided: nub and quads

Two more names describe formations by what's *missing*.

A [**nub**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nub) side is a side of the formation where a tight end
is the only receiver, attached to the line with no wide receiver outside him. "Trips nub" (the
bottom-left plate above) puts three receivers to one side and only the tight end on the other.
It's a clever shape, because it splits the formation's identity in two. The tight end side is the
**strong side** for the run game (it has the extra blocker), while the trips side is the receiver
strength (it has the extra pass-catchers). Remember the common defensive rule from [Formation
Rules](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd): *front to the tight end, coverage to the passing
strength*. Trips nub is built to make that rule hurt. The front leans one way and the coverage the
other, so a defense that sets its front to the tight end is under-manned against the receivers, and
a defense that rotates its coverage to the receivers is light against a run to the tight end.

The defense's usual answer is to keep the backside cornerback on the nub side anyway, lined up over or
just outside the tight end five to seven yards deep. From there he can come up and force a run to
that side or run with the tight end if he goes deep. Other defenses send that cornerback across to
the trips side and give the tight end to a linebacker or safety. Either way the defense has had to
*decide*, which is the point of the formation.

[**Quads**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quads) puts four receivers on one side. Only five
players can be eligible, and the line needs an eligible end on *each* side if the offense wants to
be able to throw to both, so quads almost always means empty: four receivers on one side, one on the
line on the other, nobody beside the quarterback (the 4x1 above). Keep a back beside the quarterback
and the arithmetic breaks: with nobody on the other side, the tackle becomes that end of the line,
both remaining players on the line have to stand on the quads side, and the inner one is covered and
ineligible. It's the most
extreme overload in football, and it's rare: you'll
see it in two-minute drills, on trick plays, and from offenses testing whether the defense has a
rule for it. Its value is the question it asks. A defense that hasn't practiced against four
receivers on one side has to improvise, and improvised coverage is how receivers get open.

## The condensed revolution

Everything so far might suggest the answer is always "spread out more." For about a decade, that
was roughly where NFL offenses were heading. Then, in the late 2010s, some of the most successful
offenses in the league started doing something that looked like going backward: they pulled their
receivers *in*.

A [**condensed formation**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-condensed-formation) lines its
receivers up close to the offensive line, with [reduced
splits](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) (inside the painted numbers) or even tight
ones (a few yards outside the tackle or tight end), instead of out near the sidelines. The
personnel is the same; the receivers just stand closer to the ball. (Coaches have a dialect for
this. Besides the *plus* and *minus* splits you met in [Formation
Rules](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd), you'll hear "reduced," "squeeze" and "nasty,"
the last one for a receiver only two or three yards outside the tackle or tight end.) Sean McVay's
Los Angeles Rams made it their signature in the late 2010s, Kyle Shanahan's San Francisco 49ers took
it furthest, and much of the league followed: by Next Gen Stats' count, condensed alignments went
from about 11% of NFL plays in 2016 to outnumbering wide ones in 2023.[^condensed]

That raises a question of words. Is a condensed trips formation a "spread" formation? The cleanest
way to think about it is as **two separate dials**. One dial is the *count*: how many receivers
stand on each side (2x2, 3x1, empty). The other is the *width*: how far from the ball they stand
(spread or condensed). Any count can be set at any width:

::: {#cell-fig-two-dials .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
CONDENSED_W = {"2x2": {"X": -9.0, "H": -5.9, "Y": 5.9, "Z": 9.0},      # the same players, pulled in
               "3x1": {"X": -9.0, "Y": 5.6, "H": 8.0, "Z": 10.6}}


def condense(name):
    return check_legal([p.moved(w=CONDENSED_W[name][p.key]) if p.key in CONDENSED_W[name] else p
                        for p in form(name)])


DIAL_LAT, DIAL_WIN = (-SIDELINE, SIDELINE), (-6.6, 2.6)
fig, axes = grid(2, 2, DIAL_LAT, DIAL_WIN, extra=0.42)
for r_i, name in enumerate(["2x2", "3x1"]):
    for c_i, width_name in enumerate(["spread", "condensed"]):
        ax = axes[r_i, c_i]
        p = ring_bodies(Play(form(name) if width_name == "spread" else condense(name), None, los=40,
                             to_go=None))
        fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=DIAL_LAT, window=DIAL_WIN, title=False)
        hide_yard_numbers(ax)
        for sgn in (-1, 1):
            w0 = sgn * (SIDELINE - 13.0)
            shade(ax, p, fld, [(-6.4, w0 - 1.0), (2.4, w0 - 1.0), (2.4, w0 + 1.0), (-6.4, w0 + 1.0)],
                  style.MUTED, alpha=0.10, lw=0.4)
        widest = max(abs(q.w) for q in p.players.values() if q.side == "off")
        title(ax, f"{name}, {width_name}", f"widest: {widest:.1f} yd from the ball")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.9, bottom=0.12, hspace=0.6, wspace=0.05)
ring_legend(fig)
plt.show()
```

So a condensed 3x1 is still a 3x1, and still part of the shotgun, three-receiver family the NFL
lives in; it just isn't *wide*. Broadcasters will call all four of these pictures "spread" at some
point. When this book says spread or condensed, it means the width dial.

If the condensed pictures remind you of the tight formation in the very first figure of this
chapter, they should. On paper the alignments are close. The difference is in who is standing there
and what they're for:

- **Different bodies.** The old tight formations got their blockers by bringing in a fullback or a
  second tight end, and the defense answered with linebackers. A condensed formation is usually 11
  personnel: three wide receivers. The defense still has to stay in nickel to cover them, so the
  extra defender near the ball is a nickel back (about 195 pounds) rather than a linebacker. (In 2018,
  defenses had five or more defensive backs on the field for about 94% of the Rams' snaps, as
  [Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) showed.)
- **Different threats.** A fullback or second tight end in a tight formation is mostly a blocker. A
  wide receiver in a condensed split can block, but he can also run past the defender in front of
  him or across the field, so every defender near him has to respect both.
- **One picture for everything.** The point of condensing isn't to run the ball more; it's to run
  the ball *and* throw it from a picture that doesn't tell the defense which. The four reasons below
  are all versions of that.

### 1. Room to the outside

You met the basic trade in [Formation Rules](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd), as a tell: a
reduced split often means a route toward the sideline or a block on the inside. Here's why it works.
A receiver lined up near the sideline has little grass outside him, and the cornerback covering him
knows it. The cornerback can line up inside the receiver and let the sideline guard the outside,
like a twelfth defender. A throw to that receiver on an outside-breaking route also has to travel
across most of the field. Move the receiver in toward the ball and the grass outside him becomes his,
and the same route turns into a shorter, safer throw:

::: {#cell-fig-wide-vs-condensed .cell execution_count=15}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def split_view(w_x, cb_w):
    """Left half of a 2x2 (the right half is off the picture, so legality isn't checked here)."""
    off = [Player("LT", "LT", "off", LINE_D, -2 * OL_SPLIT, label=""),
           Player("LG", "LG", "off", LINE_D, -OL_SPLIT, label=""), Player("C", "C", "off", LINE_D, 0.0, label=""),
           P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, w_x), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, w_x / 2 - 1.0)]
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.8),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, w_x / 2 - 1.6, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, cb_w), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -9.5)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None)
    p.route("X", r.out(10.0, 7.0))
    p.pass_to("X", t=1.75)
    p.highlight("X", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    return p


LAT, WIN = (-SIDELINE, 2.0), (-7.0, 15.5)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN)
for ax, (w_x, cb_w, head) in zip(axes.flat, [(-16.5, -15.6, "Wide split"), (-8.5, -9.8, "Condensed split")]):
    p = split_view(w_x, cb_w)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    shade(ax, p, fld, [(0.0, w_x - 0.8), (14.5, w_x - 0.8), (14.5, -SIDELINE), (0.0, -SIDELINE)],
          style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.10)
    (td, tw), (cd, cw) = p.pass_target_spot()
    throw = float(np.hypot(cd - td, cw - tw))
    left_after = SIDELINE + cw
    put(ax, p, fld, f"throw about {throw:.0f} yd\n{left_after:.0f} yd to the sideline\nafter the catch",
        12.6, -13.0, size=7.0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

That doesn't contradict the last chapter's split ladder. A receiver *on* the numbers, about 12 to
14 yards from the sideline, does have room to break either way; it's a receiver outside the
numbers, or one pinned into the short side of the field when the ball is on a hash, who has lost
most of his outside room. Condensing goes the other direction: it turns "some room outside" into
"more room outside than the cornerback can protect from where he's standing."

### 2. The two-way go

That leads to the second reason. A receiver with room on *both* sides of his defender has what
coaches call a [**two-way go**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-way-go): he can break inside
or outside, and the defender has to guess. Against a receiver near the sideline, the defender
doesn't guess; he takes away the inside and lets the sideline squeeze everything that breaks
outside. Against a receiver with a two-way go, a defender who leans one way gets beaten the other.

::: {#cell-fig-two-way-go .cell execution_count=16}
``` {.python .cell-code}
LAT, WIN = (-SIDELINE, 2.2), (-2.6, 10.0)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN, extra=0.42)
for ax, (w_x, head) in zip(axes.flat, [(-17.0, "Near the sideline: one way"), (-8.0, "Room both ways: two-way go")]):
    off = [P("X", "WR", LINE_D, w_x), Player("C", "C", "off", LINE_D, 0.0, label="")]
    cb_w = w_x + (1.0 if w_x < -12 else 0.0)
    p = Play(off, [D("CB", "CB", 1.4, cb_w)], los=40, to_go=None)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    if w_x < -12:

              style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.12)

        put(ax, p, fld, "taken\naway", 8.3, w_x + 6.4, size=7.0, color=style.INK_2, boxed=False)
```

The defender's position relative to the receiver, inside him, outside him or straight in front, is
called his [leverage](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd), and the quick passing game is
largely a contest of reading it. The point here is about the formation: **where a receiver lines up
decides how many ways he can go, and so how much the defender has to guess.** Slot receivers have
always had two-way gos. Condensed splits give one to the outside receivers too.

The two-way go matters most against man coverage with no help nearby, which is why you'll hear it so
much on third down. If the defense has a safety or a linebacker helping inside, the cornerback can
play outside leverage, give up the inside to his helper and stop guessing. Taking that help away,
by spreading the other defenders out or pulling them toward the run, is the offense's job.

### 3. Crack blocks

The third reason is the run game. A receiver who lines up close to the formation is *already
inside the cornerback* and right next to the defenders he wants to block, close enough to hit them
from the side. A [crack block](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) is a wide
receiver blocking back toward the ball, on a nickel back, linebacker or safety who is watching the
play and not him. It's one of the most effective blocks in football, because the defender is looking
the other way and the receiver gets a running start. From a wide split it takes too long: by the
time the receiver gets back inside, the play is over. From a condensed split he's there in a step or
two.

If that sounds like a cheap shot, the rulebook agrees with you halfway. A crack block is legal, but
only if it's above the waist and not to the head or neck: a receiver who lines up more than two
yards outside the tackle and blocks back toward the ball near the line may not go low, and doing it
costs 15 yards.[^crackback] So the receiver needs to get his eyes and hands on the front of the
defender, chest-high, which is one more reason he wants to start close to him. [Perimeter Runs and
Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) has the full rule.

Here's the classic version, a toss (the quarterback pitches the ball underhand to a back who is
already running wide) with the receiver cracking inside and a pulling lineman (one who leaves his
spot at the snap and runs along the line to block somewhere else) replacing him on the cornerback.
Coaches call that pairing *crack-and-replace*. Here the guard pulls; in other versions, like the
one in [Perimeter Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd), the tackle does:

::: {#cell-fig-crack-toss .cell execution_count=17}

``` {.python .cell-code}
                                   P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 8.6)])

             D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.2, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
             D("NB", "NB", 4.4, -6.6, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -10.2), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 10.0),
             D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -7.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 7.0)]
```

Notice the defender who got blocked. The nickel back was lined up to stop the toss, watching the
ball, and the receiver he was "covering" turned around and hit him from the side. If the nickel
starts watching the receiver instead, the receiver runs past him on a pass. That's the condensed
formation's version of the slot question from earlier in the chapter: a defender who has to worry
about the receiver *and* the run can't do both. The rest of the perimeter run game, including the
jet sweep (a receiver running across the formation at full speed who takes a handoff and keeps
going to the edge), is in [Perimeter Runs and
Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd).

### 4. Everything looks the same

The last reason is the subtlest, and for many coaches the most important. When receivers stand
close to the formation on every play, a run and a pass start from **the same picture**. The
receiver who cracks on a run is lined up exactly where he lines up to run a route on play-action
(faking the handoff, then throwing). The defense can't read the play from the splits. The
condensed formations of the late-2010s Rams and 49ers were built around exactly that: [outside
zone](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) runs (on which the whole line steps sideways
together and the back aims for the edge), crack blocks and [play-action](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)
passes, all from one look. The condensed split is also the ideal launch point for a favorite
play-action pass of those offenses: the receiver starts inside the cornerback and just outside the
linebackers, the linebackers step up to stop the fake run, and he crosses the field behind them.
A linebacker or safety who guessed "run" because the receivers were tight was guessing wrong half
the time.

Two more things come with the tight picture. A receiver eight yards from the ball can [motion](02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)
across the formation in about a second, so condensed splits and pre-snap motion go naturally together. And the more often the offense lines up this way, the less
any single snap gives away.

### What condensed gives up

Nothing in football is free, and condensing has two clear costs.

**It brings the defense in too.** Defenders line up on receivers, so when the receivers move in,
the defenders move in, and the box can get *more* crowded, not less. The spread's first benefit,
thinning the box, runs backward. Condensed offenses accept that because the receivers now block
those extra defenders, but a condensed formation against a defense that plays it well can feel
very crowded.

**It gives up horizontal stretch.** A spread formation makes defenders cover sideline to sideline; a
condensed one lets them stay closer together, so one defender can sometimes cover two receivers,
and quick throws to the outside, like screens to a receiver near the sideline, have less room. The
[horizontal stretch](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd), making defenders cover
too much width, is one of the passing game's basic weapons, and condensing trades some of it for
the other advantages.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**Condensed formations exist because the spread taught defenses to play wide.** Once defenses
learned to spread out and play the receivers from the inside, using the sideline as help, the open
space moved: it was now *outside* the receivers and in the [run
fits](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd) near the ball (each
run defender's assigned gap, which a block from an unexpected angle can wipe out). Condensing puts
the receivers where the new space is, and where they can block the defenders who are watching the
ball. It trades width for angles. It's the same idea as the spread, making the defense defend
space it would rather not, aimed at a different patch of grass.
:::

## Specialty looks

Three more formations deserve names, not because you'll see them every drive but because when you
do see them, they're asking a specific question, and you can answer it before the snap.

### Wildcat: a direct snap to someone else

In the [**wildcat**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wildcat), the ball is snapped directly to a
running back (or a receiver, or a tight end) standing where the shotgun quarterback would be, while
the real quarterback lines up as a receiver or leaves the field. Usually another back or receiver
runs in motion across the formation at the snap, so the player who takes the snap can hand it to
him, fake to him, or keep it himself.

::: {#cell-fig-wildcat .cell execution_count=18}
``` {.python .cell-code}
wc = check_legal(line5() + [P("RB", "RB", GUN, 0, "R"), P("QB", "QB", OFF_BALL, -11.8, "Q"),
                            P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -16), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
                            P("F", "RB", OFF_BALL, 9.0, "F"), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 15.5)])
wd = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
      D("SAM", "SAM", 4.2, 7.4), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -16), D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -11.8, "$"),
      D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 15.5), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0)]
wp = Play(wc, wd, los=40, to_go=None)
wp.motion("F", to=(-2.6, 1.2))
wp.run("F", [(-2.2, -3.0), (-0.6, -9.0), (3.2, -13.0), (8.5, -14.5)], absolute=True)
wp.pull("LG", [(-1.5, 1.4), (-1.5, 4.0), (1.3, 4.9)])          # the power puller leads up through the hole

ax = plt.gca()
```
